content: 1. Reporting requirements and incident protocols should be clearly established to ensure a systematic response to water quality issues. 2. A risk-based surveillance program must be defined to prioritize monitoring parameters and frequencies based on the level of risk. 3. Additional regulations tailored to small water supplies should be implemented to promote risk management practices and ensure effective monitoring. 4. In Uganda, the community-based management system has historically been the primary model for small-scale rural water supplies. However, concerns about the sustainability of these services have led the Ministry of Water and Environment to review various data sources, including national and subnational water point functionality data, barriers to effective operations, and best practices from other countries. 5. The review revealed that functionality rates of water points had stagnated at around 85% for several years, highlighting the need for sector reform. This led to the publication of the National Framework for Operation and Maintenance of Rural Water Infrastructure in Uganda (2020), which introduced professionalized area service providers to offer regular maintenance and repair services under contracts with local government water authorities. 6. In Ecuador, municipalities often delegate drinking-water service provision to small community organizations, resulting in highly variable service quality. To address data gaps, water quality testing for Escherichia coli (E. coli) was integrated into household surveys, starting with the National Survey on Employment, Unemployment, and Subemployment in 2016. 7. The inclusion of water quality indicators in the National Development Plan (2017–2021) encouraged regular water quality testing in national household surveys. By 2019, testing expanded to include water at the point of consumption, revealing that water quality was the primary barrier to achieving safely managed drinking-water services. 8. Household water treatment methods, such as boiling, and hygiene practices, including safe storage and handwashing with soap, were identified as critical interventions. In 2022, testing for E. coli and residual chlorine was incorporated into the National Survey on Child Malnutrition, providing ongoing data on microbial safety and seasonal influences on water quality. 9. Cabo Verde has made significant progress in improving rural water supply services, with access to at least basic water services increasing from 72% in 2012 to 83% in 2022. This progress is attributed to sector reforms, including the establishment of two autonomous regulatory agencies: the National Water and Sanitation Agency and the Multisector Economic Regulatory Agency. 10. These agencies have developed comprehensive regulatory mechanisms, including standards, guidelines, incentives, sanctions, and performance monitoring. A benchmarking process evaluates service providers on 15 service quality indicators and 16 economic and financial indicators, with results publicly shared. 11. In Israel, the establishment of the Israeli Water Authority in 2007 centralized planning, development, management, and regulation of the water sector, including small drinking-water suppliers. The Israeli Water Authority Council, an independent interministerial regulatory body, has facilitated coordinated planning and decision-making across multiple government ministries, improving sector cohesion and effectiveness. 12. In Uganda, the Ministry of Water and Environment has transformed six regional water and sanitation support organizations into utilities focused on small towns and rural growth centers, referred to as umbrella organizations. These utilities have improved access, service reliability, and water quality, with rural populations using uncontaminated water supplies increasing from 34% in 2015 to 56% in 2022. 13. Sustainable financing for rural water services in Uganda relies on three sources: user fees, government subsidies, and revenue from other activities such as cesspool emptying and water quality testing. Improved revenue collection efficiency and increased household connections have enhanced financial viability. 14. In the United States, over 97% of public water systems are small supplies serving 10,000 or fewer people. Capacity development for small water supply operators is mandated by the 1996 Safe Drinking Water Act Amendments, requiring states to assist public water systems in building technical, managerial, and financial capacities. 15. Operator training and certification programs vary by state, with requirements tailored to the size and complexity of water facilities. For example, in Hawaii, operators must have a high school diploma, pass a certification exam, and meet work experience requirements based on facility classification. 16. Non-state actors, such as the Rural Community Assistance Program and the National Rural Water Association, provide additional support for operator training and compliance. Circuit Riders from these organizations assist operators with maintenance, compliance, and management tasks.
